detailed_rationale:
Shree Renuka Sugars Ltd manufactures and refines sugar, and produces ethanol and cogenerated power, with Singapore-based agribusiness major Wilmar International as majority promoter (stable ~62.5% holding). Despite that strategic parentage, the balance sheet is in genuine distress: FY26 revenue fell 16% to Rs 9,169cr (from Rs 10,907cr) and the company posted a net loss of Rs 792cr, worse than FY25's Rs 300cr loss. The company has now posted losses in 7 of the last 8 reported quarters, with operating margin compressed to roughly 0.2% - effectively break-even at the operating level before interest.

Most critically, reserves have turned deeply negative (roughly Rs -2,890cr) against borrowings of about Rs 7,174cr, giving a negative book value per share of approximately Rs -12.6. Interest coverage is essentially zero (0.03x per the scorecard) - operating profit covers only a fraction of the ~Rs 736cr annual interest burden. This is a company that is, on a book basis, technically insolvent, and needs either a debt restructuring, a capital infusion, or a sustained multi-year turnaround in sugar/ethanol economics to repair its balance sheet.

India's ethanol-blending push (E20 mandate) is a genuine structural tailwind for distillery-integrated sugar producers, and Renuka does have that capacity - but this tailwind cannot be credited until it shows up in the numbers, and right now it has not offset the scale of the losses. We treat the statistically 'cheap' value score here (98.9 on our model) as a false signal - it reflects distressed pricing against a negative book value, not genuine undervaluation.
recommendation_rationale: Negative net worth and near-zero interest coverage are unambiguous balance-sheet distress signals that outweigh Wilmar's strategic backing and any ethanol-policy tailwind. This is a clear Sell; the statistical cheapness in our value score is an artifact of negative book value, not a genuine bargain.
summary: Shree Renuka Sugars is a sugar, ethanol and power company majority-owned by global agribusiness group Wilmar, but its balance sheet is under real stress - the company has posted losses in most recent quarters, its net worth has turned negative, and its operating profit does not come close to covering interest costs. While India's ethanol-blending policy is a genuine long-term tailwind for distillery-linked sugar producers, it has not yet turned around this company's financial position. We view the shares as high-risk and would not hold them.
positive_para: Wilmar International's majority ownership provides a credible, well-capitalised strategic parent that could in principle support a turnaround; the company's distillery/ethanol and cogeneration capacity positions it to benefit from India's ethanol-blending mandate if and when a turnaround materialises.
negative_para: Net worth is negative (reserves around Rs -2,890cr against Rs 7,174cr of borrowings), interest coverage is essentially zero, and the company has lost money in 7 of the last 8 quarters with FY26 losses widening to Rs 792cr. There is no evidence yet of the ethanol/policy tailwind translating into a turnaround.
reverse_dcf_judgment: With negative book value and interest coverage near zero, there is no meaningful reverse-DCF anchor - the equity value here is effectively an option on a successful balance-sheet restructuring or a sharp multi-year improvement in sugar/ethanol economics, neither of which is currently visible in the numbers.
